claim: Mutations in the discoidin domain receptor 2 gene (DDR2) are associated with human craniofacial abnormalities, such as midface hypoplasia and open fontanels.
source: Mutations in the discoidin domain receptor 2 gene (DDR2), which encodes a non-integrin collagen receptor, are associated with human craniofacial abnormalities, such as midface hypoplasia and open fontanels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature on DDR2 mutations and their clinical manifestations.

claim: Ddr2-deficient mice exhibit defects in craniofacial bones including impaired calvarial growth and frontal suture formation.
source: As will be shown, Ddr2-deficient mice exhibit defects in craniofacial bones including impaired calvarial growth and frontal suture formation, cranial base hypoplasia due to aberrant chondrogenesis and delayed ossification at growth plate synchondroses.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 1-2).

claim: Ddr2-deficient mice exhibit cranial base hypoplasia due to aberrant chondrogenesis and delayed ossification at growth plate synchondroses.
source: As will be shown, Ddr2-deficient mice exhibit defects in craniofacial bones including impaired calvarial growth and frontal suture formation, cranial base hypoplasia due to aberrant chondrogenesis and delayed ossification at growth plate synchondroses.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2-3.

claim: Defects in Ddr2-deficient mice were associated with abnormal collagen fibril organization, chondrocyte proliferation and polarization.
source: These defects were associated with abnormal collagen fibril organization, chondrocyte proliferation and polarization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including SHG imaging, EdU staining, and GM130 immunostaining presented in Figures 2-3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ddr2 is expressed in progenitor cell-enriched craniofacial regions including sutures and synchondrosis resting zone cartilage.
source: As established by localization and lineage-tracing studies, Ddr2 is expressed in progenitor cell-enriched craniofacial regions including sutures and synchondrosis resting zone cartilage, overlapping with GLI1 + cells, and contributing to chondrogenic and osteogenic lineages during skull growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-gal staining data in Ddr2-LacZ mice (Figure 4) and lineage tracing studies (Figure 5).

claim: Ddr2 expression overlaps with GLI1 + cells in craniofacial regions.
source: As established by localization and lineage-tracing studies, Ddr2 is expressed in progenitor cell-enriched craniofacial regions including sutures and synchondrosis resting zone cartilage, overlapping with GLI1 + cells, and contributing to chondrogenic and osteogenic lineages during skull growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunostaining data showing DDR2 and GLI1 colocalization (Figure 5e, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Ddr2-expressing cells contribute to chondrogenic and osteogenic lineages during skull growth.
source: As established by localization and lineage-tracing studies, Ddr2 is expressed in progenitor cell-enriched craniofacial regions including sutures and synchondrosis resting zone cartilage, overlapping with GLI1 + cells, and contributing to chondrogenic and osteogenic lineages during skull growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing experiments using Ddr2Mer-icre-Mer;Rosa26LSL-tdTomato mice (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Ddr2 is required in GLI+ skeletal progenitors for proper craniofacial morphogenesis.
source: Tissue-specific knockouts further established the requirement for Ddr2 in GLI +skeletal progenitors and chondrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by conditional knockout experiments using Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice (Figure 6).

claim: Ddr2 is required in chondrocytes for proper craniofacial morphogenesis.
source: Tissue-specific knockouts further established the requirement for Ddr2 in GLI +skeletal progenitors and chondrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by conditional knockout experiments using Col2a1-Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice (Figure 7).

claim: DDR2 is necessary for proper collagen organization in craniofacial tissues.
source: These studies establish a cellular basis for regulation of craniofacial morphogenesis by this understudied collagen receptor and suggest that DDR2 is necessary for proper collagen organization, chondrocyte proliferation, and orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and SHG imaging data showing altered collagen distribution and orientation in Ddr2-deficient mice (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: DDR2 is necessary for proper chondrocyte proliferation in craniofacial tissues.
source: These studies establish a cellular basis for regulation of craniofacial morphogenesis by this understudied collagen receptor and suggest that DDR2 is necessary for proper collagen organization, chondrocyte proliferation, and orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU staining data showing reduced proliferation in Ddr2-deficient synchondroses (Figure 2e-f, Figure 7—figure supplement 2a-b).

claim: DDR2 is necessary for proper chondrocyte orientation in craniofacial tissues.
source: These studies establish a cellular basis for regulation of craniofacial morphogenesis by this understudied collagen receptor and suggest that DDR2 is necessary for proper collagen organization, chondrocyte proliferation, and orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by GM130 immunostaining data showing disrupted chondrocyte polarity in Ddr2-deficient mice (Figure 7m).

claim: Craniofacial abnormalities affecting bone formation in the skull and face are common birth defects in humans.
source: Craniofacial abnormalities affecting bone formation in the skull and face are common birth defects in humans (Fish, 2016; Trainor and Richtsmeier, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The craniofacial skeleton forms through regulated bone growth in the calvarium synchronized with growth of the developing brain and cranial base.
source: The craniofacial skeleton forms through regulated bone growth in the calvarium synchronized with growth of the developing brain and cranial base.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in craniofacial development.

claim: Cranial sutures are the principal sites for growth of the cranial vault.
source: Cranial sutures, fibrous tissues adjoining calvarial bones, are the principal sites for growth of the cranial vault.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in craniofacial development.

claim: Sutures contain stem cells associated with several genetic markers including Gli1, Axin2, and Prrx1.
source: Sutures contain stem cells associated with several genetic markers including glioma-associated oncogene 1 (Gli1), an intermediate in hedgehog signaling, Axin-related protein 2 (Axin2), a component of the Wnt pathway, and paired related homeobox 1 (Prrx1) (Lana-Elola et al., 2007; Maruyama et al., 2016; Wilk et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Sutural stem cells allow continued calvarial growth through osteogenic differentiation and bone formation at sutural edges of the calvarial bones.
source: The current paradigm suggests that sutural stem cells allow continued calvarial growth through osteogenic differentiation and bone formation at sutural edges of the calvarial bones.
evidence: This claim represents the current understanding in the field based on existing literature.

claim: Calvarial growth is coordinated with growth of the cranial base mediated by endochondral ossification centers called synchondroses.
source: This process is coordinated with growth of the cranial base mediated by endochondral ossification centers called synchondroses.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in craniofacial development.

claim: The synchondrosis is a mirror-image growth plate with resting chondrocytes in the central zone and proliferative and hypertrophic chondrocytes on both sides.
source: Histologically, the synchondrosis is a mirror-image growth plate with resting chondrocytes in the central zone and proliferative and hypertrophic chondrocytes on both sides.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about synchondrosis structure.

claim: During endochondral ossification, resting chondrocytes in the growth plate synchondrosis undergo sequential proliferation, hypertrophic differentiation, and apoptosis before being replaced by bone.
source: During endochondral ossification, the resting chondrocytes in the growth plate synchondrosis undergo sequential proliferation, hypertrophic differentiation, and apoptosis before being replaced by bone.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about endochondral ossification.

claim: The cranial base has been implicated in many human syndromes such as craniosynostosis, Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, cleidocranial dysplasia, cleft palate, and osteogenesis imperfecta.
source: The cranial base has been implicated in many human syndromes such as craniosynostosis (premature closure of cranial sutures), Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, cleidocranial dysplasia, cleft palate, and osteogenesis imperfecta (Cheung et al., 2011; McGrath et al., 2012; Nie, 2005; Paliga et al., 2014; Tahiri et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is critical for maintenance of stem cell niches, differentiation, organ development, and remodeling.
source: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is critical for maintenance of stem cell niches, differentiation, organ development, and remodeling (Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: During craniofacial development, skeletal stem cells interact with the collagen-rich ECM through cell-surface receptors.
source: During craniofacial development, skeletal stem cells interact with the collagen-rich ECM through cell-surface receptors.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about cell-ECM interactions during development.

claim: Cell-ECM interactions regulate cell proliferation, migration, differentiation, and remodeling to control and maintain shapes of individual cranial bones and the relative proportions of skeletal elements.
source: These interactions regulate cell proliferation, migration, differentiation, and remodeling to control and maintain shapes of individual cranial bones and the relative proportions of skeletal elements (Erlebacher et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Disruption of cell-ECM interactions can cause craniofacial abnormalities.
source: Disruption of these interactions can cause craniofacial abnormalities (Lu et al., 2011; Erlebacher et al., 1995; Velleman, 2000; Kuivaniemi et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Discoidin domain receptors (DDR1 and DDR2) are a unique class of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) that mediate interactions between cells and the ECM by specifically binding triple-helical collagens.
source: Discoidin domain receptors (DDR1 and DDR2) are a unique class of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) that, together with β1 integrins, mediate interactions between cells and the ECM by specifically binding triple-helical collagens (Vogel et al., 1997; Shrivastava et al., 1997; Leitinger and Hohenester, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DDRs contain a unique discoidin (DS) domain on their extracellular surface that is homologous to discoidin I-like domain of the slime mold Dictyostelium discoideum.
source: DDRs contain a unique discoidin (DS) domain on their extracellular surface that is homologous to discoidin I-like domain of the slime mold Dictyostelium discoideum (Leitinger and Hohenester, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: DS domains are required for collagen recognition and specificity of DDRs.
source: DS domains are required for collagen recognition and specificity of DDRs such that DDR2 preferentially binds to fibrillar collagens I-III, but not nonfibrillar basement membrane type IV collagen that is exclusively recognized by DDR1 (Vogel et al., 1997; Shrivastava et al., 1997; Leitinger and Kwan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DDR2 preferentially binds to fibrillar collagens I-III.
source: DS domains are required for collagen recognition and specificity of DDRs such that DDR2 preferentially binds to fibrillar collagens I-III, but not nonfibrillar basement membrane type IV collagen that is exclusively recognized by DDR1 (Vogel et al., 1997; Shrivastava et al., 1997; Leitinger and Kwan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DDR2 does not bind to nonfibrillar basement membrane type IV collagen.
source: DS domains are required for collagen recognition and specificity of DDRs such that DDR2 preferentially binds to fibrillar collagens I-III, but not nonfibrillar basement membrane type IV collagen that is exclusively recognized by DDR1 (Vogel et al., 1997; Shrivastava et al., 1997; Leitinger and Kwan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Type IV collagen is exclusively recognized by DDR1.
source: DS domains are required for collagen recognition and specificity of DDRs such that DDR2 preferentially binds to fibrillar collagens I-III, but not nonfibrillar basement membrane type IV collagen that is exclusively recognized by DDR1 (Vogel et al., 1997; Shrivastava et al., 1997; Leitinger and Kwan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DDR2 plays an important role during human craniofacial morphogenesis, possibly being involved in skull changes occurring during the evolution of modern humans from archaic hominins.
source: DDR2 plays an important role during human craniofacial morphogenesis, possibly being involved in skull changes occurring during the evolution of modern humans from archaic hominins (Kuhlwilm and Boeckx, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: DDR2 loss of function mutations cause the autosomal recessive growth disorder, spondylo-meta-epiphyseal dysplasia, with short limbs and abnormal calcifications (SMED, SL-AC).
source: Moreover, DDR2 loss of function mutations cause the autosomal recessive growth disorder, spondylo-meta-epiphyseal dysplasia, with short limbs and abnormal calcifications (SMED, SL-AC).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about DDR2 mutations and human disease.

claim: SMED, SL-AC is associated with a number of craniofacial abnormalities including a prominent forehead, open fontanelles, hypertelorism, a short nose with a depressed nasal bridge, long philtrum and micrognathia.
source: This disorder is associated with a number of craniofacial abnormalities including a prominent forehead, open fontanelles, hypertelorism, a short nose with a depressed nasal bridge, long philtrum and micrognathia (Alkindi et al., 2014; Ali et al., 2010; Bargal et al., 2009; Mansouri et al., 2016; Ürel-Demir et al., 2018; Smithson et al., 2009; Rozovsky et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on SMED, SL-AC patients.

claim: Ddr2-deficient mice recapitulate craniofacial phenotypes seen in SMED SL-AC patients including short snout, protruding eyes, abnormal tooth development and impaired calvarial ossification.
source: Ddr2-deficient mice recapitulate craniofacial phenotypes seen in SMED SL-AC patients including short snout, protruding eyes, abnormal tooth development and impaired calvarial ossification (Ge et al., 2016; Kano et al., 2008; Labrador et al., 2001; Mohamed et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on Ddr2-deficient mice.

claim: Ddr2slie/slie mice exhibit a significant reduction (12%) in skull length mainly due to shortening of the nasal bone (NB), cranial vault (CV), and anterior and posterior cranial base (ACB and PCB).
source: Our analysis along the anterior-posterior (AP) axis revealed a significant reduction (12%) in skull length (SL) mainly due to shortening of the nasal bone (NB), cranial vault (CV), and anterior and posterior cranial base (ACB and PCB) in Ddr2-deficient mice compared with WT littermates (Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear measurements on micro-CT scans presented in Figure 1a-c.

claim: Ddr2slie/slie mice exhibit an increase in anterior skull width without any change in skull height.
source: In addition, we detected an increase in anterior skull width without any change in skull height (Figure 1d–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 1d-e.

claim: Frontal bone thickness was reduced by 55% in Ddr2slie/slie mice.
source: Interestingly, frontal bone thickness was reduced by 55% with Ddr2 deficiency; however, no significant differences were observed in the thickness of parietal or occipital bones (Figure 1f–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of calvarial bone thickness presented in Figure 1f-g.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the thickness of parietal or occipital bones in Ddr2slie/slie mice.
source: Interestingly, frontal bone thickness was reduced by 55% with Ddr2 deficiency; however, no significant differences were observed in the thickness of parietal or occipital bones (Figure 1f–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 1f-g.

claim: Ddr2-deficient mice show defective formation of frontal sutures.
source: Further analysis using Alcian blue and Alizarin red whole mount and H&E staining of 2-week-old skulls showed defective formation of frontal sutures in Ddr2-deficient mice (defect in 3/3 mice examined).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological staining data presented in Figure 1h-i.

claim: Coronal and lambdoid sutures had a normal morphology in Ddr2-deficient mice.
source: In contrast, coronal and lambdoid sutures had a normal morphology (Figure 1h–i).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological staining data presented in Figure 1h-i.

claim: Ddr2-deficient calvaria had a reduced calvarial bone marrow cavity that was most prominent in the anterior skull bones.
source: Ddr2-deficient calvaria also had a reduced calvarial bone marrow cavity that was most prominent in the anterior skull bones (Figure 1f and i).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 1f and i.

claim: Reduced mineralization in the posterior frontal suture region was seen in 6/10 skulls from 3-month-old Ddr2slie/slie mice.
source: Consistent with results from 2-week-old mice, reduced mineralization in the posterior frontal suture region was also seen in most skulls from 3-month-old Ddr2slie/slie mice, although some phenotypic variability was observed at this age with 6/10 skulls affected (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by micro-CT data presented in Figure 1b.

claim: The ISS and SOS were abnormally wide in Ddr2slie/slie mice compared with WT littermates.
source: Our analysis showed that the ISS and SOS were abnormally wide in Ddr2slie/slie mice compared with WT littermates (Figure 2a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements on H&E staining and micro-CT scans presented in Figure 2a-d.

claim: At 2 months, the width of the ISS was increased by 187% in Ddr2slie/slie mice.
source: At 2 months, the width of the ISS and SOS was increased by 187% and 23%; respectively, while a significant increase in the height was only observed in the SOS of knockout mice (12%) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 2b.

claim: At 2 months, the width of the SOS was increased by 23% in Ddr2slie/slie mice.
source: At 2 months, the width of the ISS and SOS was increased by 187% and 23%; respectively, while a significant increase in the height was only observed in the SOS of knockout mice (12%) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 2b.

claim: A significant increase in the height was only observed in the SOS (12%) of Ddr2slie/slie mice.
source: At 2 months, the width of the ISS and SOS was increased by 187% and 23%; respectively, while a significant increase in the height was only observed in the SOS of knockout mice (12%) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 2b.

claim: Growth of basisphenoid bone was significantly inhibited (reduced by 14%) in Ddr2slie/slie mice.
source: Accordingly, growth of basisphenoid bone was significantly inhibited in the knockout mice (reduced by 14%) (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 2c.

claim: The basio-occipital (BO) bone was significantly affected in Ddr2slie/slie mice but to lesser extent than basisphenoid bone.
source: The basio-occipital (BO) bone was also significantly affected but to lesser extent.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 2c.

claim: No major difference was seen in the presphenoid (PS) bone in Ddr2slie/slie mice.
source: No major difference was seen in the presphenoid (PS) bone (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 2c.

claim: Ddr2-deficient synchondroses showed severe defects in chondrocyte organization associated with loss of the columnar arrangement of proliferative chondrocytes.
source: H&E staining of 2-week-old skulls revealed that the Ddr2-deficient synchondroses, particularly ISS, showed severe defects in chondrocyte organization associated with loss of the columnar arrangement of proliferative chondrocytes (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data presented in Figure 2d.

claim: EdU + chondrocytes were significantly reduced in Ddr2-deficient synchondroses: 55% in ISS and 26% in SOS, compared with WT controls.
source: EdU staining (shown in green) indicated labeling mainly in the proliferative chondrocyte zone of ISS and SOS (Figure 2e, white arrowheads); however, EdU +chondrocytes were significantly reduced in Ddr2-deficient synchondroses: 55% in ISS and 26% in SOS, compared with WT controls (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU staining data presented in Figure 2e-f.

claim: TUNEL assay did not detect differences in apoptosis between Ddr2-deficient and control mice in either ISS or SOS regions.
source: We also performed TUNEL assay to measure apoptosis, but did not detect differences between Ddr2-deficient and control mice in either ISS or SOS regions (Figure 2g–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL assay data presented in Figure 2g-h.

claim: Staining for cleaved caspase 3 was not affected by Ddr2 deficiency.
source: Consistent with this result, staining for cleaved caspase 3 was also not affected by Ddr2 deficiency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In wild-type mice, Col II was homogenously distributed in the cartilage matrix around chondrocytes.
source: In wild-type mice, immunofluorescent staining of type II collagen was homogenously distributed in the cartilage matrix around chondrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3a.

claim: Col II was unevenly distributed in Ddr2-deficient synchondroses where more intense territorial matrix staining was observed around small clusters of chondrocytes with diminished staining in the interterritorial matrix.
source: However, Col II was unevenly distributed in Ddr2-deficient synchondroses where more intense territorial matrix staining was observed around small clusters of chondrocytes with diminished staining in the interterritorial matrix (Figure 3a, arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3a.

claim: In control synchondroses, collagen fibrils were evenly distributed and generally oriented along the A-P axis of the ISS.
source: In control synchondroses, collagen fibrils were evenly distributed and generally oriented along the A-P axis of the ISS.
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG imaging data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fibrils in Ddr2-deficient synchondroses were more concentrated adjacent to cells and had a more randomized orientation as reflected by a dramatic decrease in anisotropy relative to WT controls.
source: In contrast, fibrils in Ddr2-deficient synchondroses were more concentrated adjacent to cells and had a more randomized orientation as reflected by a dramatic decrease in anisotropy relative to WT controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG imaging and anisotropy measurements presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No consistent differences in Col X staining intensity were observed between WT and Ddr2slie/slie mice.
source: Type X collagen immunostaining showed a specific signal in the hypertrophic zone although no consistent differences in staining intensity were observed between WT and Ddr2slie/slie mice (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3b.

claim: For COL I, no differences in staining intensity were observed when WT and Ddr2slie/slie mice were compared.
source: For COL I, no differences in staining intensity were observed when WT and Ddr2slie/slie mice were compared.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: IBSP staining was reduced in hypertrophic chondrocytes and primary spongiosa in Ddr2-deficient SOS compared with WT.
source: However, IBSP staining was reduced in hypertrophic chondrocytes and primary spongiosa in Ddr2-deficient SOS compared with WT, suggesting defective bone formation and mineralization, although these differences were not seen in the ISS.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a-b.

claim: During fetal development, Ddr2 expression was first detected at E11.5.
source: During fetal development, LacZ activity was first detected at E11.5 (not seen at E9.5 -not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-gal staining data from Ddr2+/LacZ mice.

claim: At E11.5, Ddr2 expression was detected in the developing midface including the median and lateral nasal process (MNP and LNP), maxillary and mandibular processes, and around eyes.
source: The whole mount staining at this time revealed broad Ddr2 expression in the developing midface including the median and lateral nasal process (MNP and LNP), maxillary and mandibular processes, and around eyes (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole mount X-gal staining data presented in Figure 4a.

claim: At E13.5, LacZ activity was detected in cartilage primordia of the cranial base, tongue mesenchyme, nasal septum, and Meckel's cartilage in the developing mandible, and developing tooth buds.
source: Using frozen sections of the E13.5 embryonic head, LacZ activity was detected in cartilage primordia of the cranial base, tongue mesenchyme, nasal septum, and Meckel's cartilage in the developing mandible, and, as previously reported, developing tooth buds (Mohamed et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-gal staining data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: No LacZ activity was detected in the developing brain.
source: However, no LacZ activity was detected in the developing brain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-gal staining data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Whole mounts of Ddr2+/LacZ skulls from newborn mice showed broad Ddr2 expression across the calvarial surface with preferential enrichment in cranial sutures.
source: Whole mounts of Ddr2+/LacZ skulls from newborn mice showed broad Ddr2 expression across the calvarial surface with preferential enrichment in cranial sutures.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole mount X-gal staining data presented in Figure 4a.

claim: Ddr2 expression became more restricted to sutures in 3-month-old adult mice.
source: This distribution became more restricted to sutures in 3-month-old adult mice (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole mount X-gal staining data presented in Figure 4a.

claim: Frozen sections of neonatal Ddr2+/LacZ skulls revealed Ddr2 expression in the suture mesenchyme, periosteum of flanking bones, and dura mater on the ventral surface of calvaria.
source: Frozen sections of neonatal Ddr2+/LacZ skulls revealed Ddr2 expression in the suture mesenchyme, periosteum of flanking bones, and dura mater on the ventral surface of calvaria (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-gal staining data on frozen sections presented in Figure 4b.

claim: Suture and periosteal expression were seen in adult calvaria as well as in cells lining the bone marrow.
source: Suture and periosteal expression were also seen in adult calvaria as well as in cells lining the bone marrow (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-gal staining data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: LacZ activity was not seen in osteocytes.
source: However, LacZ activity was not seen in osteocytes, the terminally differentiated cells inside calvarial bones.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-gal staining data.

claim: Ddr2 expression is highest during early stages of osteoblast differentiation.
source: This indicates that Ddr2 expression is highest during early stages of osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Ddr2 is expressed in sutures and periosteum but not in osteocytes.

claim: Ddr2 expression was detected in synchondroses, primarily located in the resting (RZ) and proliferative chondrocyte (PZ) zone but low or undetected in terminal hypertrophic chondrocytes (HZ).
source: Ddr2 expression was also detected in synchondroses, primarily located in the resting (RZ) and proliferative chondrocyte (PZ) zone but low or undetected in terminal hypertrophic chondrocytes (HZ), and in the associated bone marrow and periosteum (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-gal staining data presented in Figure 4c.

claim: Ddr2 expression was highest in regions enriched in skeletal progenitor cells including cranial sutures, periosteum and dura mater and resting chondrocytes.
source: Overall, Ddr2 expression was highest in regions enriched in skeletal progenitor cells including cranial sutures, periosteum and dura mater and resting chondrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the pattern of X-gal staining observed in Ddr2+/LacZ mice (Figure 4).

claim: Ddr2 has functions in skeletal progenitor cells which contribute to development of the craniofacial skeleton.
source: This suggests that Ddr2 has functions in skeletal progenitor cells which contribute to development of the craniofacial skeleton.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the localization of Ddr2 expression in progenitor-enriched regions.

claim: At day 5, tdTomato labeling was detected in a few cells in the cranial suture mesenchyme and in developing periosteum and dura mater of flanking calvarial bones.
source: At day 5, frozen sections revealed tdTomato labeling in a few cells in the cranial suture mesenchyme and in developing periosteum and dura mater of flanking calvarial bones (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: Two weeks after tamoxifen induction, labeling was evident in cranial sutures, periosteum, and dura mater.
source: Two weeks later, labeling was evident in cranial sutures, periosteum, and dura mater.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: Over a 2-month chase period, labeling became intense in cranial suture mesenchyme, in the lining cells in the bone marrow of flanking calvarial bones, and in osteocytes.
source: Over a 2-month chase period, labeling became intense in cranial suture mesenchyme, where undifferentiated cells reside, in the lining cells in the bone marrow of flanking calvarial bones, and in osteocytes (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The osteoblasts, osteocytes, and bone marrow-lining cells responsible for calvarial bone formation are derived from Ddr2-expressing cells.
source: Therefore, the osteoblasts, osteocytes, and bone marrow-lining cells responsible for calvarial bone formation are derived from Ddr2-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data showing tdTomato-labeled cells in these cell types (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).

claim: At day 5, TdTomato labeling in synchondroses was detected in some cells in resting and proliferative zones, where Ddr2-labeled cells were either single cells dominant in the resting zone or pairs of daughter cells dominant in proliferative zone.
source: At day 5, TdTomato labeling was detected in some cells in resting and proliferative zones, where Ddr2-labeled cells were either single cells dominant in the resting zone or pairs of daughter cells dominant in proliferative zone.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: Ddr2 showed no labeling in hypertrophic chondrocytes at day 5.
source: However, Ddr2 showed no labeling in hypertrophic chondrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: By two weeks, progeny of Ddr2-labeled cells were seen in all chondrocyte lineages and associated bone marrow.
source: By two weeks, progeny of Ddr2-labeled cells were seen in all chondrocyte lineages and associated bone marrow.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: By 2 months, labeled cells persisted in the resting chondrocyte zone and formed columns of cells extending through proliferative and hypertrophic zones.
source: By 2 months, labeled cells persisted in the resting chondrocyte zone and formed columns of cells extending through proliferative and hypertrophic zones.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Progeny of Ddr2-expressing cells were seen on the surface of trabecular bone, in the bone marrow and in osteocytes within the cortical bone of the cranial base.
source: Progeny of Ddr2-expressing cells were also seen on the surface of trabecular bone, in the bone marrow and in osteocytes within the cortical bone of the cranial base (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Ddr2 is expressed in cell populations within cranial sutures and synchondroses having features of skeletal progenitor cells.
source: Together, our results indicate that Ddr2 is expressed in cell populations within cranial sutures and synchondroses having features of skeletal progenitor cells, but the identity of these cells still needs to be determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by localization and lineage tracing data (Figures 4-5).

claim: GLI1 is associated with stem/progenitor cells in cranial sutures.
source: GLI1, a mediator of hedgehog signaling, is associated with stem/progenitor cells in cranial sutures (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Gli1CreERT labeling was detected in cranial sutures in a pattern like that seen for Ddr2.
source: As previously reported (Zhao et al., 2015), Gli1CreERT labeling was detected in cranial sutures in a pattern like that seen for Ddr2 (Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5d.

claim: Gli1CreERT showed labeling in all chondrocyte lineages of cranial base synchondroses, with high concentration in resting and proliferative chondrocytes.
source: Gli1CreERT also showed labeling in all chondrocyte lineages of cranial base synchondroses, with high concentration in resting and proliferative chondrocytes (Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5d.

claim: Gli1 expression is not restricted to cells in cranial sutures or subchondral metaphyseal bone but is also in growth plate chondrocytes of synchondroses.
source: This suggests that Gli1 expression is not restricted to cells in cranial sutures or subchondral metaphyseal bone as previously reported, but it is also in growth plate chondrocytes of synchondroses.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data presented in Figure 5d.

claim: A high degree of colocalization was observed between DDR2 and GLI1 in select suture cells and adjacent periosteum.
source: A high degree of colocalization was observed in select suture cells and adjacent periosteum and in the central resting zone and hypertrophic regions of the SOS and ISS with a subfraction of GLI1 + cells (68–78 percent) also being DDR2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunostaining data presented in Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: 68-78 percent of GLI1+ cells in synchondroses are also DDR2+.
source: A high degree of colocalization was observed in select suture cells and adjacent periosteum and in the central resting zone and hypertrophic regions of the SOS and ISS with a subfraction of GLI1 + cells (68–78 percent) also being DDR2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of colocalization presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tamoxifen-treated Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice had craniofacial abnormalities of similar type and magnitude to those seen in global Ddr2 knockouts.
source: Tamoxifen-treated Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice had craniofacial abnormalities of similar type and magnitude to those seen in global Ddr2 knockouts.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of phenotypes between Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice (Figure 6) and Ddr2slie/slie mice (Figures 1-2).

claim: Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice had significantly reduced skull length (11%) due to shortening in the nasal bones, cranial vault, and posterior cranial base.
source: Conditional knockout mice had significantly reduced skull length (11%) due to shortening in the nasal bones, cranial vault, and posterior cranial base (Figure 6c–e)
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 6c-e.

claim: Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice had reduced anterior skull width in the absence of significant changes in skull height at most sites except posterior cranial height that was reduced by approximately 5%.
source: and reduced anterior skull width in the absence of significant changes in skull height at most sites except posterior cranial height that was reduced by approximately 5% (Figure 6f–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 6f-g.

claim: Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice had thin frontal bones.
source: Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice also had thin frontal bones (Figure 6d and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 6d and h.

claim: Delayed mineralization in the posterior portion of the frontal suture was observed in 5 of 10 Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice.
source: Also, like Ddr2slie/slie mice, delayed mineralization in the posterior portion of the frontal suture was observed in 5 of 10 mutant skulls; this was not seen in Ddr2fl/fl mice (n=10, Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by micro-CT data presented in Figure 6d.

claim: Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice had abnormally wide cranial base synchondroses with greatest changes seen in the ISS.
source: Analyzing 2-week-old skulls, Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice also had abnormally wide cranial base synchondroses with greatest changes seen in the ISS (Figure 6i–k).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and imaging data presented in Figure 6i-k.

claim: Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice showed a significant shortening in cranial base bones, including presphenoid (13%), basisphenoid (~15%), and basio-occipital bones (11%).
source: Similarly, mutant mice showed a significant shortening in cranial base bones, including presphenoid (13%), basisphenoid (~15%), and basio-occipital bones (11%), suggesting impaired endochondral ossification at 3 months (Figure 6m–p).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 6m-p.

claim: DDR2 functions in GLI1-positive cells to control suture formation/calvarial bone mineralization as well as endochondral growth in the cranial base.
source: Together, these results are consistent with the GLI1 distribution we observed in cranial sutures and synchondroses and suggest that DDR2 functions in GLI1-positive cells to both control suture formation/calvarial bone mineralization as well as endochondral growth in the cranial base.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phenotype of Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl mice (Figure 6).

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice exhibited growth defects compared with littermate controls.
source: At birth, mutant mice were viable and indistinguishable from their control littermates, but as they matured, Col2a1-Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice exhibited growth defects compared with littermate controls (Ddr2fl/fl).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of Col2a1-Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice.

claim: Col2a1-Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice had significantly reduced AP skull growth and increased anterior and posterior skull width and reduced posterior cranial height.
source: Linear measurements on micro-CT scans of 3-month-old skulls (n=10) showed significantly reduced AP skull growth and increased anterior and posterior skull width and reduced posterior cranial height in Col2a1-Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice (Figure 7a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 7a-d.

claim: The reduction in AP skull length in Col2a1-Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice (7%) did not reach levels seen in Ddr2slie/slie (12%) or Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl skulls (11%).
source: However, the reduction in AP skull length (7%) did not reach levels seen in Ddr2slie/slie (12%) or Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl skulls (11%) (Figure 1 versus 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of measurements across different mouse models (Figures 1, 6, 7).

claim: Col2a1Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice exhibited growth defects in endochondral bones, mainly BS and BO contributing to cranial base hypoplasia.
source: Col2a1Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice also exhibited growth defects in endochondral bones, mainly BS and BO contributing to cranial base hypoplasia (Figure 7h).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 7h.

claim: The ISS was significantly wider (270%) and higher (32%) in Col2a1Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice.
source: In addition, the ISS was significantly wider (270%) and higher (32%) (Figure 7g and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 7f-g.

claim: The width and height of the SOS in Col2a1Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice was increased, but to a lesser extent than for the ISS.
source: The width and height of the SOS in Gli1CreERT;Ddr2fl/fl was also increased, but to a lesser extent than for the ISS (Figure 7g).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 7g. Note: The text appears to have a typo referring to Gli1CreERT;Ddr2fl/fl when discussing Col2a1Cre results.

claim: Conditional deletion of Ddr2 in chondrocytes minimally affected the AP growth of cranial vault (decreased by 2.5%).
source: In contrast, conditional deletion of Ddr2 in chondrocytes minimally affected the AP growth of cranial vault (decreased by 2.5%) (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 7b.

claim: Col2a1Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice exhibited significant thinning in the frontal bone (56%) as compared with controls.
source: Col2a1Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice exhibited significant thinning in the frontal bone (56%) as compared with controls (Figure 7a and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 7a and e.

claim: The parietal bone (11.4%) and occipital bone (12%) showed a moderate decrease in thickness in Col2a1Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice.
source: Unlike Ddr2slie/slie or Gli1CreERT;Ddr2fl/fl mice, the parietal bone (11.4%,) and occipital bone (12%) also showed a moderate decrease in thickness-11.4 and 12%, respectively (Figure 7e).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 7e.

claim: Conditional knockout in Col2a1-Cre lineages did not affect cranial sutures which were indistinguishable from Ddr2f/f controls.
source: Significantly, conditional knockout in Col2a1-Cre lineages did not affect cranial sutures which were indistinguishable from Ddr2f/f controls (n=10 mice/genotype, Figure 7a).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 7a.

claim: Ddr2 has separate functions in both suture mesenchyme and cranial base chondrocytes.
source: This clearly resolves functions of Ddr2 in cranial base that were disrupted in Ddr2slie/slie, Gli1CreERT;Ddr2fl/fl and Col2a1Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice from functions in sutures that were only disrupted in Ddr2slie/slie and Gli1CreERT;Ddr2fl/fl animals and establishes separate functions for Ddr2 in both suture mesenchyme and cranial base chondrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of phenotypes across different conditional knockout models (Figures 6-7).

claim: Conditional deletion of Ddr2 in mature osteoblasts using BglapCre did not affect skull length, cranial sutures, or the cranial base in 3-month-old mice.
source: In contrast to results with Gli1CreERT;Ddr2fl/fl and Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice, conditional deletion of Ddr2 in mature osteoblasts using BglapCre did not affect skull length, cranial sutures, or the cranial base in 3-month-old mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Craniofacial functions of Ddr2 are restricted to skeletal progenitors and chondrocytes rather than mature bone forming cells.
source: These results are consistent with craniofacial functions of Ddr2 being restricted to skeletal progenitors and chondrocytes rather than mature bone forming cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of phenotypes between Gli1CreERT;Ddr2fl/fl, Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl, and BglapCre;Ddr2fl/fl mice (Figures 6-7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: At birth, no significant differences in synchondroses were seen between Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mutant and control littermates.
source: At birth, no significant differences in synchondroses were seen between mutant and control littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course histological analysis presented in Figure 7l.

claim: As endochondral ossification progressed, the resting zone became progressively narrower in controls while expanding at the expense of the proliferative and hypertrophic zones in Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice.
source: However, as endochondral ossification progressed, the resting zone (highlighted with red lines) became progressively narrower in controls while expanding at the expense of the proliferative and hypertrophic zones in Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice (Figure 7l).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course histological analysis presented in Figure 7l.

claim: Synchondrosis widening in Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice could not be explained by increased cell proliferation which was reduced in ISS and SOS.
source: As was the case in Ddr2slie/slie mice (Figure 2), synchondrosis widening could not be explained by increased cell proliferation which was reduced in ISS and SOS (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU staining data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Type II collagen distribution was abnormal in Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice with a selective loss of staining in the inter-territorial matrix.
source: Also, as was seen in Ddr2slie/slie mice, type II collagen distribution was abnormal in Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice with a selective loss of staining in the inter-territorial matrix.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2c.

claim: In Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice, there was an increase in average spacing between cells.
source: In Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice, we also observed an increase in average spacing between cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2c, Figure 7n).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 7n and Figure 7—figure supplement 2c.

claim: P14 Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice formed an ectopic hypertrophic zone on the ventral side of the ISS at right angles to the normal synchondrosis axis.
source: Intriguingly, P14 Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice formed an ectopic hypertrophic zone on the ventral side of the ISS at right angles to the normal synchondrosis axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis presented in Figure 7l.

claim: MicroCT images of 3-month-old Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice showed W-shaped synchondroses, suggesting ectopic endochondral ossification taking place in the ventral side of the ISS.
source: MicroCT images of 3-month-old mice also showed W-shaped synchondroses in Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice (Figure 7f), suggesting ectopic endochondral ossification taking place in the ventral side of the ISS.
evidence: This claim is supported by micro-CT imaging data presented in Figure 7f.

claim: The W-shaped synchondrosis phenotype was seen in 8 out of 10 Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl mice examined.
source: This phenotype was seen in 8 out of 10 mutant mice examined.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of multiple mice.

claim: In control mice, GM130 immunostaining showed well-defined, localized staining adjacent to the nucleus, indicating that positional information was retained within the growth plate.
source: In control mice, immunostaining of GM130 showed well-defined, localized staining adjacent to the nucleus, indicating that positional information was retained within the growth plate (Figure 7m).
evidence: This claim is supported by GM130 immunostaining data presented in Figure 7m.

claim: In Col2a1Cre;Ddr2fl/fl synchondroses, GM130 immunostaining was disorganized, suggesting that chondrocyte polarization was disrupted.
source: In mutant synchondroses; however, GM130 immunostaining was disorganized, suggesting that chondrocyte polarization was disrupted.
evidence: This claim is supported by GM130 immunostaining data presented in Figure 7m.

claim: Proper DDR2 signaling is important for specification of cell polarity possibly through interaction with the cartilage extracellular matrix.
source: Together, our findings indicate that proper DDR2 signaling is important for specification of cell polarity possibly through interaction with the cartilage extracellular matrix; however, a direct role of Ddr2 on chondrocyte polarity cannot be excluded.
evidence: This claim is based on the observed disruption of chondrocyte polarity in Ddr2-deficient mice.

claim: DDR2 controls suture formation, frontal bone thickness and anterior/posterior growth of the skull.
source: Furthermore, as shown by global and conditional inactivation approaches, DDR2 controls suture formation, frontal bone thickness and anterior/posterior growth of the skull.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis of Ddr2slie/slie, Gli1CreERT; Ddr2fl/fl, and Col2a1Cre; Ddr2fl/fl mice (Figures 1-2, 6-7).

claim: DDR2 functions involve activity in different cell populations.
source: Notably, these DDR2 functions involve activity in different cell populations and are correlated with changes in collagen organization and chondrocyte polarity.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of phenotypes in different conditional knockout models (Figures 6-7).

claim: DDR2 functions are correlated with changes in collagen organization and chondrocyte polarity.
source: Notably, these DDR2 functions involve activity in different cell populations and are correlated with changes in collagen organization and chondrocyte polarity.
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG imaging, immunofluorescence, and GM130 staining data (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 7m).

claim: DDR2 may function by controlling properties of the ECM such as collagen distribution, fibril orientation and stiffness, which in turn alters cell behavior via regulation of integrin signaling.
source: Although the basis for DDR2 actions on cranial and skeletal development are not well-understood, we hypothesize that it may function by controlling properties of the ECM such as collagen distribution, fibril orientation and stiffness, which in turn alters cell behavior via regulation of integrin signaling.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and existing literature.

claim: DDR2 in cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) increases tumor stiffness by reorganizing type I collagen fibrils at the tumor-stromal boundary, thereby promoting lung metastasis of breast tumors.
source: For example, DDR2 in cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) increases tumor stiffness by reorganizing type I collagen fibrils at the tumor-stromal boundary, thereby promoting lung metastasis of breast tumors.
evidence: This claim is based on existing literature on DDR2 function in cancer.

claim: ECM changes associated with DDR2 in CAFs are associated with increased integrin activity and mechanotransduction.
source: These ECM changes are associated with increased integrin activity and mechanotransduction by CAFs (Bayer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of DDR2 in trauma-induced heterotopic ossification (HO) in mice was associated with decreased collagen fibril orientation and dramatic inhibition of HO.
source: Also, in a recent collaborative study on trauma-induced heterotopic ossification (HO) in mice, we showed that loss of DDR2 was associated with decreased collagen fibril orientation as measured by SHG as well as dramatic inhibition of HO (Pagani et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a collaborative study.

claim: The loss of collagen alignment in HO was accompanied by a reduction in integrin signaling as measured by reduced FAK phosphorylation, decreased nuclear translocation of TAZ and reduced YAP/TAZ signaling.
source: The loss of collagen alignment was accompanied by a reduction in integrin signaling as measured by reduced FAK phosphorylation, decreased nuclear translocation of TAZ and reduced YAP/TAZ signaling, consistent with DDR2 being required for force transduction, subsequent osteoblast differentiation and HO.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a collaborative study (Pagani et al., 2022).

claim: Col2a1expDmm/Dmm mice harboring a mutation in the C-propeptide globular domain of type II collagen have defects in the assembly and folding of type II collagen, that alter collagen distribution/orientation.
source: Both Col2a1expDmm/Dmm mice harboring a mutation in the C-propeptide globular domain of type II collagen (Col2a1) (Pace et al., 1997) as well as mice containing an R992C mutation associated with spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia Arita et al., 2015 have defects in the assembly and folding of type II collagen, that alter collagen distribution/orientation (Arita et al., 2015; Brown et al., 1981; Pace et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Col2a1 mutant mice are dwarf, have a shortened vertebral column and small rib cage as well as craniofacial defects characterized by skull dysmorphogenesis, reduced skull length, reduced cranial base length, cleft palate, and short mandible.
source: In both cases, mutant mice have a similar phenotype to Ddr2-nulls; they are dwarf, have a shortened vertebral column and small rib cage as well as craniofacial defects characterized by skull dysmorphogenesis, reduced skull length, reduced cranial base length, cleft palate, and short mandible.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on Col2a1 mutant mice.

claim: Mice harboring the R992C mutation exhibit disrupted chondrocyte polarity.
source: Interestingly, mice harboring the R992C mutation also exhibit disrupted chondrocyte polarity (Arita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Altered distribution of cartilage matrix was reported in a SMED, SL-AC patient.
source: Most importantly, the altered distribution of cartilage matrix was also reported in a SMED, SL-AC patient (Borochowitz et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a case report.

claim: Histological analysis of the resting zone of costochondral cartilage from a SMED, SL-AC patient showed abnormally distributed chondrocytes with noticeable dark staining in surrounding matrix filling lacunar space.
source: Histological analysis of the resting zone of costochondral cartilage from a SMED, SL-AC patient showed abnormally distributed chondrocytes with noticeable dark staining in surrounding matrix filling lacunar space (Borochowitz et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a case report.

claim: The altered distribution of cartilage matrix highlights the similarity between histopathological features of SMED, SL-AC patient samples and Ddr2-deficient mice.
source: The altered distribution of cartilage matrix highlights the similarity between histopathological features of the patient samples and our results in Ddr2-deficient mice, and provides important insights into potential mechanisms underlying Ddr2 regulation of bone development mediated by changes in ECM organization.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison between patient data and mouse model data.

claim: Ddr2 has a critical function in skeletal progenitor cells, including GLI1 + cells, and chondrocytes to control bone formation and cartilage growth during postnatal growth of the craniofacial skeleton.
source: In summary, this study establishes a critical function of Ddr2 in skeletal progenitor cells, including GLI1 + cells, and chondrocytes to control bone formation and cartilage growth during postnatal growth of the craniofacial skeleton, and advances our understanding of the roles of cell-matrix interactions in craniofacial morphogenesis.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study supported by data in Figures 1-7.

claim: The findings provide insight into the cellular basis of cranial defects in SMED SL-AC patients.
source: Our findings provide further insight into the cellular basis of cranial defects in SMED SL-AC patients as well as evolutionary changes in craniofacial structure related to altered DDR2 activity.
evidence: This claim is based on the similarity between mouse model phenotypes and human patient phenotypes.

claim: The findings provide insight into evolutionary changes in craniofacial structure related to altered DDR2 activity.
source: Our findings provide further insight into the cellular basis of cranial defects in SMED SL-AC patients as well as evolutionary changes in craniofacial structure related to altered DDR2 activity.
evidence: This claim is based on the known role of DDR2 in human evolution (Kuhlwilm and Boeckx, 2019) and the findings of this study.
